extracted.intended_audience: readers of a 19th-century mathematical journal; advanced undergraduate/graduate students and researchers in classical analytic and synthetic geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of classical theorems, definitions, and constructive/analytical methods in plane and solid geometry (conics, higher-order curves, surfaces, diameters, polar/polar-plane constructions), with worked solutions and criteria for classification. Primarily aimed at solving and understanding geometry problems by analytic methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion of distinction for second-degree curves (classification by signs and parallels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of a second-degree curve (ellipse, parabola, hyperbola) determined by the sign arrangement of four quantities A, C, B, B’ (distances from origin to certain conjugate points) and by parallelism relations of certain constructed lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If of the four lines/quantities A, C, B, B’ one or three are negative — equivalently three of the four points A, C, B, B’ lie on the boundary of one of a pair of opposite axis-angles and one on the other — then the curve is necessarily a hyperbola. If none, two, or four are negative (i.e. all lie on the boundary of one angle, or two on one and two on its opposite), the curve may be hyperbola, ellipse, or parabola: (a) if BC and ADB’ are parallel the curve is a parabola; (b) otherwise distinguish ellipse vs hyperbola by imagining, with B fixed, the motion required of B’ to make AB’ and CB parallel — if B’ must be moved towards the origin the curve is an ellipse; if away from the origin the curve is a hyperbola. (This criterion connects algebraic sign information b^2 − 4ac and related quantities to geometric position/parallelism.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of vanishing coefficients for conics
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for geometric interpretation when one or more coefficients of the general second-degree form vanish (degeneration cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: if the form degenerates to ay^2 + cz^2 + f = 0 then D = 0 and E = 0, so the polar line of the origin is at infinite distance (the origin is the centre); AD and CE finite imply A = 0 and C = 0 (either axis is the central conjugate of the other), and the curve is referred to conjugate diameters. Other vanishing-coefficient cases are treated similarly: one inspects which polar/central quantities become infinite/zero and interprets the resulting geometric degeneration (axes, centres, indeterminate points).

rubrics_metrics.name: Converse polar construction determining a unique conic
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two axes (conjugate diameters) and a polar line to the origin parallel to a given line BB’, one and only one second-order curve is determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: take two points B and B' one on each axis, and choose the polar of the origin to be a line parallel to BB'; then one curve of the second order is determined and only one — this is the converse of the theorem that associates polar lines/central conjugates to a given conic. The surrounding discussion shows how the line-equations of certain conjugate lines (AB', CB, DE) relate through distances OA, OB, OC, OD, OB', OE to yield the curve equation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chasles' polar-planes collinearity theorem (for quadrics)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a surface of the second degree, any triangle placed arbitrarily yields three polar planes whose intersections with the opposite sides are three collinear points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement: any triangle (in arbitrary position relative to a quadric) — the polar planes of the three vertices meet the opposite sides in three points which lie on one straight line. Special cases (triangle in a principal plane, two points at infinite distance) reduce to previously given planar theorems. Use this as a geometric test/consequence of polarity with respect to a quadric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of diameter of a curve (generalized)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diameter of a curve: the locus of the midpoints of a family of parallel chords; equivalently, the line (straight or curved) passing through the midpoints of a series of parallel chords.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the working definition used to pose and solve problems: 'Given the equation of a curve and the angular coefficient of a straight line, find the locus of the midpoints of all chords parallel to that line.' Two methods to find this locus are provided (abscissa-sum root theory and origin-translation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method I for finding diameters (abscissae-sum/root relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Method based on the property that if x1 and x2 are abscissae of two points on a straight line then x1 + x2 = 2x (x midpoint), and using elimination/elaboration from the curve's algebraic equation to derive the locus equation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated for third-order curves: denote intersections of a chord with the curve by roots x1,x2,x3 and form symmetric relations; use the coefficient of x^2 (or the appropriate symmetric coefficient) and relations like x1 + x2 + x3 = ... to eliminate variables and obtain an equation for (X, Y) the midpoint. For third-order curves the resulting diameters are in general curves of the same (third) order. The method requires elimination of auxiliary roots and uses theory of roots of algebraic equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method II for finding diameters (translate origin to midpoint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal method based on translating the origin to the midpoint of a chord so that the chord's endpoints acquire equal and opposite coordinates; impose that the transformed curve's equation admits roots ±a (or that linear terms vanish appropriately) to characterize the midpoint locus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: remove origin to (h,k), write transformed equations for curve and line family, eliminate the dependent variable, and introduce the condition that the transformed equation factor as (2°−m^2)(2^... ) so that the two roots are equal and opposite; equivalently, for conics the diameter equation is obtained by equating to zero the coefficient of the first power (the linear term) after translation. Example: applying to a particular curve produced a diameter equation of sixth order; for second-degree curves the condition simplifies and yields the classical diameter equations by setting the coefficient of the linear term to zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order-preservation result for diameters of third-order curves
rubrics_metrics.description: Diameters of third-order curves are, in general, curves of the same (third) order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the algebraic elimination in Method I/II applied to a general cubic plane curve, one obtains an equation of third order for the locus of midpoints of parallel chords, i.e. diameters need not be straight lines and generally have same algebraic order as the original curve. (Authors note the method applies to second and third orders but 'not (it would seem) to those of higher orders' for that particular approach.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for the local position of a surface relative to its tangent plane (second-derivative test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given surface F(x,y,z)=0, compute the quadratic form built from second derivatives at a point; the sign of a specific expression determines whether the surface near the point lies entirely on one side of the tangent plane or partly on both sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let partial second-derivatives be denoted suitably (U,V,W, etc. in the text). The expression (written in the paper as an explicit symmetric combination of second derivatives) when positive implies the surface near (x,y,z) lies entirely on one side of the tangent plane (the normal-section is an ellipse); when negative the surface lies partly on both sides (normal-section is a hyperbola). If the expression equals zero, the section is a parabola (or two parallel lines) and the surface is developable (this differential condition is the equation of developable surfaces). The criterion holds for rectangular or oblique axes (note in-text remark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gregory/plane-section criterion for quadrics (ellipse vs hyperbola)
rubrics_metrics.description: The type (ellipse or hyperbola) of the planar section of a quadric is determined by the sign of a specific quadratic expression in directional cosines formed from second derivatives (an explicit formula given in the paper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the indicated expression (a symmetric function of second derivatives and direction-cosines of the cutting plane) is positive then the section is an ellipse and the surface lies on one side of the tangent plane; if negative the section is a hyperbola and the surface crosses the tangent plane. If zero, the section is a parabola (or pair of parallel lines). The paper shows how this reduces to the earlier given second-derivative test and cites Gregory's Solid Geometry for reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equation of a straight line in oblique axes via constant projection ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: In oblique three-dimensional axes, a straight line through a fixed point (a,b,c) can be represented by the property that the ratios of its projections on the coordinate axes to the line's length are constant; this yields parametric equations with constants l, m, n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let (a,b,c) be a fixed point and (x,y,z) a variable point on the line; denote the distance between them by ρ. Projections of ρ on axes are x−a, y−b, z−c; if the constant ratios are l,m,n then (x−a)/l = (y−b)/m = (z−c)/n = ρ, giving the equations of the straight line in oblique axes. Use these to derive straight-line equations analogous to rectangular-axis parametric forms but accounting for non-orthogonality via cosines of ordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developable surfaces characterization (zero of the second-derivative expression)
rubrics_metrics.description: A surface is developable if and only if the specific second-derivative expression (same as in the tangent-plane criterion) equals zero at the point; then the normal-section degenerates and locally the surface lies on one side in a limiting sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the quadratic-form expression (given explicitly in the paper) vanishes, the plane-section by the tangent direction is a parabola or two parallel lines; this differential equation is the condition for a developable surface (reference: Cambridge Mathematical Journal vol. iv, p. 154). Hence checking this expression provides a test for developability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Result: polar-planes of triangle in principal plane with two infinite points reduce to planar polar theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: If a triangle lies in a principal plane of a quadric and two of its vertices are at infinite distance, the general Chasles polar-planes theorem specializes to the planar theorem previously given about polars and conjugate diameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this specialization to reduce three-dimensional polarity statements to known planar polar/diameter relations: it provides a consistency check and a method to derive planar results from the general polar-plane theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical rule for obtaining diameter equation for conics by translation
rubrics_metrics.description: For conics, translate origin to midpoint of chord; the transformed conic's linear coefficient (first-power term) must vanish for the chord to be bisected by the new origin — equate this coefficient to zero to obtain the diameter's equation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard short method (noted in the text) used in treatises: after substituting x→x+h, y→y+k and expanding the conic equation, set the coefficient of x (or the linear term in the relevant variable) to zero to ensure roots are equal and opposite; solve the resulting relation between h and k to obtain the diameter locus. This avoids dividing by quadratic factors and heavy elimination for second-degree curves.
